title: Vesak, the fifth time
hookLine: one full moon for his birth, awakening and passing
tomorrow: after he woke up, who heard his first sermon, and where?

cards: Paper lanterns strung across a temple courtyard. A line of kids pouring scoops of water over a small statue of the baby Buddha. Lamps lit at dusk.
That's Vesak, and here's the answer to yesterday's question: in Theravada tradition, one full moon holds three of the Buddha's biggest days, his birth, his awakening and his passing.
Some East Asian communities keep the birthday on a day of its own. Either way, this is the fifth time this path has reached it. So we start at the end of the story, under two trees.

teach.b: The Mahaparinibbana Sutta tells it. The Buddha, old and ill, reaches Kusinara and lies down on his right side between twin sala trees.
Then the trees burst into bloom out of season, and the sutta says their blossoms fall over his body, with flowers and music from the sky as well. A beautiful scene, and the Buddha turns it around.
He tells Ananda that this is not how he is truly honored. Whoever lives the Dhamma, practicing it properly, small things and great, that one honors him with the highest honor.
Here's the teaching Buddhists draw from that night.
There are two kinds of offering: offering things, lamps and flowers and incense, and offering practice. Both are real, and tradition holds the second one higher.
It's why Vesak has both: lanterns in the courtyard, and people taking the precepts, some keeping extra ones for the day.
So the night comes down to this: the Buddha, dying, under blossoms falling just for him, said the flowers weren't the point. Now look back at this block with that in mind.
Few wants, room to breathe, three jewels, your vow, said aloud, a life of practice. None of those is a lamp. All of them are the other offering.
Five Vesaks on this path, five years of lamps, and what the lamps stand for is the days in between.

how: At Vesak, Buddhists visit temples, light lamps and lanterns, offer flowers, and take the precepts, some keeping extra precepts for the day; in some communities people pour water over a small statue of the baby Buddha.

o: a spring harvest feast held at the temple
the full moon of his birth, awakening and passing
the night the Buddha gave his very first sermon

games.q: the last night and the festival — tap the pairs.
p: where the Buddha lay down at the end
heard what the highest honor is

s: the Buddha called the falling blossoms the highest honor
he told Ananda the highest honor is living the Dhamma, practicing it properly.
in Theravada tradition Vesak marks birth, awakening and passing
one full moon for all three; some East Asian communities keep the birthday on its own day.
at Kusinara, the sala trees bloomed in their usual season
the sutta says they bloomed out of season and dropped their blossoms over him.

games.q: at the temple Vesak, your aunt spends all morning arranging flowers; your uncle skips the flowers and keeps extra precepts all day. who is honoring the Buddha?
o: both; but under the sala trees, living the Dhamma was the highest.
your aunt; flowers and lamps are what Vesak is really for.
your uncle; the Buddha told people to stop offering flowers.
games.why: the blossoms fell and the Buddha didn't send them away; he told Ananda that practicing the Dhamma honors him most. two offerings, one higher.

practice: If you have candles or tea lights and a safe place, light five, one for each Vesak on this path; if not, set out five small things in a row. As you light or set out each one, name one thing from these years you'll keep doing.
Then sit with the five in front of you, and watch the light, or the row, hold still.

wordCard.voice: Vesak: the full moon of the Buddha's birth, awakening and passing, honored with lamps, and with practice, puja of both kinds.

orig.note: Pali: honor, offering, whether of things like lamps and flowers, or of practice.

carryVoice: Take this along: five years of lamps, and the days of practice they stand for. One of seven in the festival year.

sources.ref: Digha Nikaya 16 (Mahaparinibbana Sutta: the twin sala trees and the highest honor)
